# Charter

## Use cases

### Shared understanding before the next iteration

A human and an agent finish a change holding different mental models of it,
and the next iteration starts from that mismatch. explain-diff closes the gap
before the loop repeats: one guide states what the system does now that it did
not before, which decisions are load-bearing, what the implications are, and
which questions remain open - then helps the human compose the reply that
starts the next round.

### Durable engineering processes

Humans and agents working in engineering use grimore to build durable
engineering processes without coaxing agents into operating effectively -
across code development, process optimization, and design. The project
exists so that alignment between humans and agents produces better tools.

### Reading the project's decisions without code access

A reader with no way into the repository still needs what the store knows: an
agent drafting release notes with no checkout, a reviewer handed a file in a
ticket, a subagent with no filesystem access. The same artifact serves a
contributor coming back from weeks on other projects who wants the project's
current beliefs in one piece rather than a directory to navigate. grim render
emits a single self-contained markdown bundle carrying every live component,
ordered coherently and stamped with the store and commit it came from, so the
reader receives something they can be handed.

### Catching up after time away

A contributor returning after days or weeks needs to know what changed. grim
render --digest --since answers it directly: every component added, promoted,
abandoned, or superseded since a given date, in the order the work landed,
each carrying the spec it came from or the commit that carried it - without
reading a single dated document end to end. The order follows the landings
rather than the component types, because a returning reader is reconstructing
a sequence of changes, and grouping by type scatters one pull request across
four separate places.

## Constraints

### No emojis in output

No emoji appears anywhere in generated output or in the authoring guidance
that produces it - plain text labels only. This is a hard constraint on
templates and skill instructions alike rather than a style preference, so that
output stays legible in terminals, diffs, screen readers, and print without
depending on font coverage.

### Generated pages make no external requests

A generated guide is a single self-contained file: styles, scripts, and any
diagram runtime are inlined, and the page issues no network request when
opened. The constraint keeps a guide readable offline, on a locked-down
machine, and years later when whatever host it might have referenced is gone.

### No file paths or code in component prose

Note bodies state subsystem facts in prose and never name file paths or embed
code snippets, both of which rot silently when files move. The
machine-readable paths frontmatter carries that information instead, where the
touched-path guard can act on it and a rename shows up as a visible
frontmatter change rather than a quietly wrong sentence.

### grim is a single-file, uv-runnable script

grim ships as one Python file, runnable through uv with no install step, no
daemon, and no dependency heavier than a YAML parser; adopting projects vendor
that single file. The constraint keeps adoption to a copy rather than a
package install, and it is why path-level granularity inside grim is
unavailable - every verb lives in the same file, so a path glob cannot
distinguish them.

### Zero-setup consumption

Current documentation must be readable with no build step, no toolchain, and
no account - the repository's web view and an agent holding only a checkout
both count as consumers. This is a hard requirement, and it is what forced
rendered views to be committed rather than generated in CI, along with the
merge discipline that keeps them honest.

### Cross-platform across agent consumers

grimore must work with different agents as consumers. It cannot be a tool
that only works in Claude Code, or Codex, or any single harness -
cross-platform support across agent consumers is a standing requirement of
the project, not a later portability effort.

### Human exports are deterministic in their declared inputs

A human export must be byte-identical when regenerated from the same declared
inputs, and nothing outside them - filesystem order, locale, or the time of
the run - may reach the output. The bundle's inputs are the live store, the
configuration governing ordering and render mapping, and the revision it
stamps. The digest's are all of those plus the resolved default-branch
revision, the since-date, and the index of which specs claim which components.
They are enumerated separately because the two exports read different things,
and a guarantee naming only the store would be false for both.

This is weaker than the guarantee the committed rendered view carries, which
grim check enforces by byte-comparing a fresh render. No gate compares an
export, so this constraint is held by tests rather than by a check, and it
exists to make output reproducible for a reader rather than to keep a gate
honest.

### The committed rendered view is byte-deterministic

Compiling the rendered view twice from the same store must produce
byte-identical output. Ordering within every rendered file is by date then id
ascending, and nothing in that output may depend on filesystem order, locale,
or the time of the run. Verification rests on this: grim check re-renders and
byte-compares, so any nondeterminism would turn the check into a random
failure. The guarantee is scoped to the committed artifact rather than to the
command that writes it, because that command may also emit output which is not
the committed view, is compiled from more than the store, and carries its own
weaker guarantee.

## Non-goals

### Bug-finding and review judgments

explain-diff explains intent and implications; it does not judge code or hunt
for bugs. A guide says what changed, why, which decisions are load-bearing and
what remains open - it never reports a defect or rates quality. Excluded
because mixing the two changes how the output is read: a document that
sometimes judges invites the reader to treat silence as approval, and code
review is a separate job with a separate standard of evidence.

### Hosted publishing of change guides

explain-diff writes a self-contained local HTML file and does not publish it
to any hosted surface; hosted publishing may be added later as an option, but
local HTML stays canonical. Excluded because a self-contained file needs no
account, no network, and no retention policy - and a change guide routinely
embeds code that has not been reviewed for disclosure.

### Multi-diff comparisons, timelines, and PDF

explain-diff explains one diff. Comparing several diffs side by side,
rendering history timelines across a series of changes, and PDF generation
beyond what the print stylesheet already produces are all excluded. Excluded
as YAGNI: each is a distinct product with its own navigation and state, and
the print CSS already covers the one export anyone actually asked for.

### Automatic external-store pointer writes

finish-docs does not write pointer or status records into external knowledge
and tracking stores automatically; keeping such a store in sync remains a
session-level habit. Excluded because automatic writes would couple the
reconciliation pass to a specific external tool that not every adopting
project has, and that coupling is hard to undo once workflows depend on it.
Revisit after v1, once the manual habit has shown what is actually worth
writing.

### Full staleness tripwire

Coverage reporting, path-hygiene tooling that detects stale or renamed
`paths:` globs, and any semantic comparison of a diff against doc content are
out of scope for v1. The minimal touched-path guard ships instead, and is
deliberately crude: it cannot report what fraction of the codebase is
documented, cannot notice when a declared glob stops matching anything, and
cannot tell a meaningful change from a trivial one. Deferred because each
addition needs either a semantic model of the diff or a maintenance surface of
its own, and neither earns its cost before the basic guard has been lived
with.

### Multi-context glossaries

One glossary per repository. The CONTEXT-MAP pattern, where a word carries
different definitions in different bounded contexts, is excluded from v1: it
would require every term to declare a context, every consumer to know which
context it reads in, and the Avoid-term lint to become context-aware. Excluded
because a repository whose glossary genuinely needs two conflicting
definitions of one word has a naming problem the glossary should force it to
resolve, not a tooling gap.

### A rejected component status

Components have three statuses - draft, current, superseded - and no fourth
for options considered and turned down. A rejected alternative is recorded
inside the body of the component that records the decision actually taken,
where a reader meets it alongside the reasoning, rather than as a separate
component that renders nowhere and accumulates in the store. Excluded because
a status that never appears in any consumer output is bookkeeping, not
documentation.

### Semantic drift detection beyond supersede edges

Status banners on specs and plans track explicit supersede edges only. A
decision reversed by a fresh component carrying no `supersedes:` edge fires no
banner, and grimore does not try to infer such reversals by comparing
component content. Excluded because that inference is a semantic judgment that
would be either unreliable or expensive, and edge-writing at branch finish is
a reviewed step precisely so the graph stays honest rather than guessed.

### A host-abstraction framework

Cross-compatible packaging will make the existing Grimore workflows install,
load, and describe equivalent actions in Claude Code and Codex, but it will
not introduce an abstraction layer that models every tool, invocation syntax,
or interaction primitive across agent harnesses. That redesign is excluded
because the current portability gaps are narrow enough to remove directly,
while a framework would add a maintained compatibility surface before the
project has evidence that more than targeted wording and provenance changes
are needed.

### Static-site generator wiring

Integration with a particular static-site generator - theme wiring, navigation
config, build hooks, deployment - is excluded. The boundary is that grim's
site-ready output stops at clean markdown, and whatever a project already uses
consumes it from there. Excluded because every generator wants its own
frontmatter and directory conventions, so adopting one would either force that
choice on every project or grow a plugin surface per generator.

### The static-site markdown tree

The site-ready markdown tree is deferred. Its shape - a file per component or
a file per render target, carrying frontmatter a generator will read or none
at all - is a decision worth making against a real publishing target rather
than guessing at one, and no such target exists yet. Deferred rather than
rejected: nongoal-static-site-generator-wiring fixes where the boundary sits
when the tree arrives, stopping short of wiring any particular generator.
